What's driving the price of oil/gas down?

Financial analyst here. I would shy away from explanations based on lower demand for oil, rather the issue is largely related to the big supply of oil at the moment.

Taking a step back: A key element here is the long running assumption that OPEC (especially Saudi Arabia) would always be the swing producer, meaning that they would adjust their output somewhat up or down in order to maintain a stable oil price. OPEC has been able to do this for quite some time, and still maintain a strong market share in the global oil market.

However, in recent years the shale oil revolution (notably in the US) has been eating away at the market share of OPEC, something they (again, especially Saudi Arabia) really dislikes. So, in a bid to squeeze out competition, OPEC (SA) decided in late 2014 to increase production and put a lot of downwards pressure on the oil price. Saudi has a much lower break even price than most of the world's oil producers, so they can handle a low oil price better than most countries, and hopefully (for SA) make non-OPEC oil production less -or non-profitable.

In an nutshell, what's happening now is a price war. Saudi wants to get rid of competition and they're willing to lose money on their national budget for a while in order to maintain their market share and the power of OPEC as a price setting cartel. I could also add that the increased production is not something that every OPEC member is comfortable with, since they depend heavily on oil revenue to balance their budget. Venezuela is one example of this. Also, day rates for oil tankers have skyrocketed, since very few expected the extra volumes of oil, and tanker companies can hence charge a premium.

Another question is where all this oil is going... Well, a lot of it goes to the regular clients; Europe, China, Japan, India and so on. China has actually been eating up a lot of the extra and cheap oil, since it's looking to fill up its strategic inventories of crude oil. Search for "China Strategic Petroleum Reserves" to learn more.

On your question on the 'missing barrels' this is often a mathematical problem. We're not talking about physical barrels of oil vanishing from the docks here, rather (as you pointed out) the numbers when comparing supply and demand for a period not adding up.

Example: IEA (International Energy Agency) posts regular reports on the oil market where they make statistics and forecasts on supply and demand of oil (they don't make oil price forecasts, but that's a different story)

Now, in theory, if you buy oil you can use that for consumption or storage. Therefore, the supply of oil in a year should be equal to the demand plus changes in oil storage/inventories.

In practice however it's not that simple. For starters, finding data for oil production and oil exports is relatively easy. For most countries in the western world, inventory data is also readily available on a weekly basis. However, data quality on demand is less transparent. You can't ask an entire country how much oil they demand on a weekly basis since there are a number of issues affecting this (refinery maintenance schedules, amount of vehicle driving etc.). Also, some countries such as China does not even publish its inventory data, so that make balancing the supply and demand data even more difficult.

What IEA does is that they collect as much and as good data on supply, demand and inventories as possible. Then, after a lot of number crunching, they KINDOFF make it all add up, but not perfectly. Keep in mind that even historical US inventory numbers get revised almost weekly, so getting perfect data across the board here is next to impossible. I would like to add though that when IEA makes revisions to its historical numbers it is most often on the demand side.

So on your question of what my opinion is: I would say 'missing barrels' makes sense considering that 1) we're collecting data from a number of sources 2) that data is never perfect 3) any data can be revised afterwards and 3) some data is difficult to accurately record (i.e. end user demand).

P.S.: As I mentioned earlier in this comment, we're not talking about barrels disappearing into thin air, but oil volumes somehow unrecorded or unaccounted for. An example of this can be Iraqi oil production by ISIS. While this oil is being sold (mostly domestically, but some of it going to Turkey as well from what I understand), actual and reliable data on this does not exist.
